The word for "pineapple" in most languages is "ananas". Ananas is also a synonym for pineapple in English. The word "ananas" is derived from the name of the fruit in the Guarani language of South America, proximate to where the plant is indigenous. The word "banana", on the other hand, is from its name in the Wolof language of West Africa. (Incidentally, the herb originates nowhere near this; instead coming from South East Asia.) While both words entered English via Portugese, and both refer to tropical fruits, there seems to be no genealogical relationship between the source languages (happy for someone to prove me wrong on this!) Consequently, the words appear to be false cognates.

According to modern botanical science, pineapples and bananas in deed belong to different families (Bromeliaceae and Musaceae, respectively). But if we go according to genetic/phylogenetic relations, then both belong to monocots, and more specifically a subgroup of that, commelinids. That means they are less distantly related to each other than eg. pineapple<>asparagus or banana<>lilies. But Bromeliaceae belongs to the order Poales, which includes also Poaceae, the grasses This means that pineapples are more closely related to grasses, eg. wheat than to bananas.

If we want to take a comparable relation as between pineapple<>banana among dicotyledynous plants then the age of last common ancestor should be known... I have no good idea, picking from Wikipedia I get perhaps 90-100-? million years. Uh, picking at random, order Cucurbitales is 107 million years old, and cucumber belongs to it (family Cucurbitaceae). Another family in the order is Begoniaceae, and that includes, surprisingly, the begonia houseplants.
